items.title: UK GDPR, Article 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data
items.locator: Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation, 5(1)(d) accuracy, 5(1)(e) storage limitation, 5(2) accountability
items.quote: adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed
items.why: The binding rule. Personal data must be adequate as well as limited, accurate and where necessary kept up to date, and kept in identifiable form no longer than necessary. Amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (5(1)(b), 5(1)(e) cross-reference, 5(3)); the page shows no known outstanding effects. Points (c) and (d) are unamended.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 25: Data protection by design and by default
items.quote: only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed
items.why: Makes minimisation a design duty, met by technical and organisational measures and applied by default to the amount collected, the extent of processing, the storage period and accessibility. Supports building the data standard into the system and not only into a policy. Amended 5 February 2026 (children: paragraphs 1A, 1B, 4, 5); no known outstanding effects.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How should we assess security and data minimisation in AI?
items.locator: Sections 'What considerations about the data minimisation principle do we need to make?', 'How should we minimise personal data in the training stage?', 'How should we balance data minimisation and statistical accuracy?'
items.quote: You must not collect personal data on the off-chance that it might be useful in the future
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. Says the default of data scientists may be to collect as much as possible; minimisation must be considered from design and in procurement due diligence; some techniques require balancing minimisation against statistically accurate and non-discriminatory models; if sufficient accuracy is achievable with fewer data points or fewer individuals, use fewer. Carries the banner: under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act. The page shows no publication date; the year is the one shown on the sibling accuracy chapter (15 March 2023).

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What do we need to know about accuracy and statistical accuracy?
items.locator: Sections 'What is the difference between accuracy in data protection law and statistical accuracy in AI?' and 'What should we do about statistical accuracy post-deployment?'
items.quote: You should regularly assess drift and retrain the model on new data where necessary.
items.why: Separates the legal accuracy principle (applies to inputs and outputs) from statistical accuracy; outputs that are inferences should be recorded as such, with provenance. Supports watching quality over time: populations change, thresholds for retraining should be documented, and supplier claims tested at procurement. Carries the banner: under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.quote: Do not retain personal information indefinitely, or just in case it is useful in the future.
items.why: Source of the figure (p.15: retention usually one or two years after the job requisition was closed). What the regulator found in practice: most providers had assessed the minimum data needed and some recorded a justification for each field (p.14); several intended to keep candidate databases indefinitely and did not weed them (pp.15-16); one restarted its one-year period on every update (p.17). Recruitment only; the audits were consensual.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, artificial intelligence toolkit: Data minimisation
items.locator: Three control measures: review of relevance at each stage; ongoing monitoring and testing; documented retention policy and schedule
items.quote: Remove or erase training data that is no longer required (eg because it is out of date and no longer predictively useful).
items.why: What the regulator's auditors look for: justification for keeping each kind of information, a standard checklist of features and retention, automated validation of incoming data, monitoring that raises alerts, and a retention schedule with evidence it is followed. Carries the 'under review' banner; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year it was read.

items.title: A guide to the data protection principles. Principle (c): Data minimisation
items.locator: 'At a glance'; sections 'How do we decide what is adequate, relevant and limited?' and 'When could we be processing inadequate personal data?'
items.quote: You should periodically review your processing to check that the personal data you hold is still relevant and adequate for your purposes
items.why: Shows the principle cuts both ways: adequate means sufficient to fulfil the purpose, so too little data is also a failure. This is the legal footing for the tension between minimal and representative data. Carries the 'under review' banner; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year it was read.

items.title: Information Commissioner's Office response to the consultation series on generative AI: Accuracy of training data and model outputs
items.locator: Sections 'Original call for evidence' and 'Key points from the responses'
items.quote: the developer should curate the training data accordingly to ensure sufficient accuracy for the purpose for which it is processed
items.why: The regulator's position on generative AI: the accuracy needed depends on the purpose, and developers should know whether training data is factual, historical, inference, opinion or AI-generated. Records industry objections that accuracy of training data cannot be verified. A consultation response, not guidance. The page shows no date; the year is taken from the series it reports. Its count of responses is internally inconsistent and is not relied on.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 3.6 'Privacy-Enhanced', p.17; see also MAP 2.3 (p.27) and Appendix B (p.38)
items.quote: techniques can result in a loss in accuracy, affecting decisions about fairness and other values in certain domains
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary United States framework that names the same trade-off: data-minimising methods support privacy but, where data is sparse, can cost accuracy and affect fairness. MAP 2.3 asks that data collection and selection be documented for availability, representativeness and suitability. Not law in the UK.

items.title: Operationalizing the Legal Principle of Data Minimization for Personalization
items.publisher: arXiv (paper in Proceedings of the 43rd International ACM SIGIR Conference); A. J. Biega, P. Potash, H. Daumé III, F. Diaz, M. Finck
items.quote: the performance decrease incurred by data minimization might not be substantial, but that it might disparately impact different users
items.why: Research evidence for the tension the brief describes: in recommender systems, minimising data cost little on average but the loss fell unevenly across users. Abstract read only; one domain, so it shows the risk exists and not how large it is elsewhere. The authors' own free copy.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 10: Data and data governance
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 10(1)-(4) and (6); para 5 shown as deleted
items.quote: shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose
items.why: The one binding rule that states the criterion's standard almost word for word, and applies to all training, validation and testing data for high-risk systems, not only personal data. Para 2 lists the governance practices expected (origin of data, preparation, assumptions, bias examination, gaps). The first-pass log found this page unreliable; it now states the consolidation date and marks paragraphs 1 and 6 AMENDED and paragraph 5 DELETED. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (EUR-Lex consolidation as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal; EUR-Lex itself returned an empty page. EU law: it reaches UK firms only where they place systems on the EU market or their output is used there. No application date is stated here because none was read on this page.

items.title: Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Prudential Regulation Authority, Bank of England
items.locator: Principle 3.2 'The use of data' (a)-(c), PDF p. 21; Principle 2.3 'Policies and procedures' (data quality management procedures), PDF pp. 15-17; para 1.5
items.quote: The model development process should demonstrate that the data used to develop the model are suitable for the intended use
items.why: A UK regulator's expectation on data fed to models, wider than personal data: data must be suitable, representative of the customers the model is used for and free of inappropriate bias; where it is not representative the impact must be assessed and the model treated as more uncertain. Firms need written rules for data quality, accuracy and relevance. Limits: sector-specific (banks, building societies and designated investment firms); supervisory expectation, not legislation; in effect from 17 May 2024. Already cited elsewhere in the library for governance passages.

items.title: The Government Data Quality Framework
items.locator: 'Data quality principles' 1-2; 'The data lifecycle'; 'Data quality dimensions'
items.quote: It is unlikely that data will be equally fit for all purposes.
items.why: The UK public sector's own standard for data quality: principles, a lifecycle view of where quality fails (including accuracy decaying over time and missing documentation), and dimensions against which quality is measured and tracked. Supports the criterion's higher levels (measured quality, monitored over time) and the point that quality is judged against a purpose. Limits: written for government bodies, voluntary for others, published 2020 and not AI-specific.

items.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612)
items.locator: para 3.13, p. 36 (PDF p. 38); summary para 16, p. 10; paras 3.12-3.14
items.quote: Access to good-quality data was identified as a barrier to implementing AI by 62% of the 87 government bodies responding to our survey.
items.why: Audit evidence that data quality is the practical constraint on AI: most surveyed government bodies named it as a barrier, and the auditor records that fixing data quality across government 'remains slow and difficult'. Limits: central government only; a survey of bodies' own views (the report describes the position 'as at autumn 2023'); about ability to adopt AI, not about harm to individuals. Already cited elsewhere for other passages.

items.title: Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification
items.publisher: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, vol. 81 (J. Buolamwini and T. Gebru)
items.quote: is underrepresented in benchmark datasets can nonetheless be subjected to frequent targeting
items.why: The best-known peer-reviewed evidence that unrepresentative data produces unequal results. Two standard face datasets were 79.6% and 86.2% lighter-skinned; three commercial systems misclassified darker-skinned women at error rates up to 34.7%, against at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned men (abstract). It is why the criterion asks for representative data and ties data quality to fairness testing. Limits: one task (gender classification from faces), three commercial products, a test set of 1,270 people; conference paper.

items.title: "Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work": Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI
items.publisher: Google Research (N. Sambasivan and others; ACM SIGCHI 2021)
items.quote: Data cascades are pervasive (92% prevalence), invisible, delayed, but often avoidable.
items.why: Peer-reviewed interview study of 53 AI practitioners in India, East and West Africa and the United States. Poor data practice early on caused compounding problems later that were hard to see when they began; the authors report 92% prevalence. Supports treating data quality as something to be monitored with alerts, not cleaned once. Limits: abstract only read in this pass, on the authors' employer's publications page; a qualitative sample, none from the UK; the publisher's page was not opened.
